# Education in Germany
Education in Germany is primarily the responsibility of the federal states (Länder), reflecting their constitutional sovereignty. The German education system is notable for its early stratification at the secondary level into various school types: Gymnasium (preparing students for university with the Abitur exam), Realschule, Hauptschule, Gesamtschule (comprehensive schools), and Sonderschule or Förderschule for students with special educational needs. Gymnasium typically lasts until grades 12 or 13, culminating in the Abitur, though recent reforms experimented with shortening this period. The dual education system (Duale Ausbildung) combines vocational training with classroom education and is highly regarded, emphasizing practical skills alongside academic knowledge.
Primary education generally lasts four years (six years in some states), followed by the route selection for secondary education, heavily influenced by academic performance and teacher recommendations. The school system includes public and private schools (Ersatzschulen), with growing private school attendance yet significant state subsidies ensuring wide accessibility. Higher education encompasses universities (Universitäten) with doctoral rights and universities of applied sciences (Fachhochschulen), focusing more on practical applications. University admission is predominantly via the Abitur, though alternative pathways exist, including aptitude tests and vocational qualifications. Public universities typically do not charge tuition fees, with semester contributions covering administrative costs. German universities emphasize academic freedom and research, with the Humboldt model underpinning their structure. Despite regional disparities and social stratifications affecting educational attainment, Germany maintains strong international rankings and robust research infrastructures.
